lines.text: The one-eyed man was Garrow. Wren's father. He had come south alone, on Skeld trails along the edge of the White, looking for us.
Father? What are you doing here?
Bram sent me. He said, find the boy and bring him home. Fast.
There's an army coming to Greyhollow, my lord. Three thousand men. They'll reach the gate in five days. Maybe four.
That's impossible. An army takes a month to march that far.
It does. This one left the day you rode into Aldcrown.
The day I rode into Aldcrown, Vance had smiled at me from the cathedral steps, and waved. Now I knew why.
The summons had never been about the Stone. It was a hook. Pull the hollow-born south, away from his people, and march an army north behind him.
And it's Penhallow leading them. His men in orange, the King's in crimson. He opened his own lands to them, so they could march around Kesting.
Penhallow. The handsome lord with the flickering ring, who had bathed in my bathhouse and eaten at my table.
But the Old Bear has declared for you. He had it shouted from every wall in Kesting. Kesting stands with the boy, and any man who disagrees can come and say so.
Halvard was gathering every man he had. Lady Ysolde had sent hers already. Bram had the Skeld, and Saltmouth, and the village. Against three thousand.
And we were standing in Penhallow's own country, with his riders on every road.
Disguises, my lord. I suggest pilgrims. Nobody looks closely at pilgrims, in case they ask for money.
So for three days, seven pilgrims and a one-eyed guide walked north through Penhallow's country, singing hymns. Oswin knew all the words. That worried me.
I was drunk for ten years, my lord. Drunks hear a great many sermons. Mostly from the floor.
On the third day, Penhallow's riders stopped us at a bridge, and looked at every face.
Pilgrims, sir, to the shrine at Kesting. My brother is simple, and my sister is mute.
I was the simple brother. Ilse was the mute sister. She has never forgiven Tamsin.
The rider looked at me. Then at the poster in his hand. Then at a goat on the far bank. Then, slowly, he waved us through.
That night, Garrow led us off the road and up into the hills, toward a line of white on the horizon.
The road is eight days to Greyhollow, with Penhallow on every mile of it. The White is four. If we live.
Then we live.
The Lord Who Measured Zero. Chapter one hundred and sixteen, coming soon.
